messages.author: e6ac6506bddc9816
messages.subject: Tree size and phylogenetic sampling
parts:
I have some conceptual questions about BioGeoBears usage. My goal is to use DEC and DEC+J models on a large tree of ~4,000 species, and then break the tree up into small clades and repeat analyses. 

What is the smallest size tree before it becomes unprudent to use this approach, because of loss of power? (As in Davis et al. 2013: BiSSE loses power after ~300 species). I saw in Matzke (2013; PhD thesis) the smallest tree size used in Chapter 3 had 5 species; should I take this to mean models implemented in BioGeoBears are not strongly affected by tree size?

My group is poorly sampled (maybe 30% of the total number of species). From reading the literature my impression is that there isn't a single common way to deal with incomplete sampling, such as adding sampling fractions to a BiSSE analysis in diversitree. Am I correct in this impression? My immediate thought to deal with this is to randomly prune tips and get some estimate of robustness of the results as if to simulate incomplete sampling (on an already incompletely sampled tree, yes). 

Thank you! Sorry for the BiSSE comparisons- I am familiar with BiSSE and diversitree but I am new to biogeographic models.

messages.author: 665b3d97beb30882
messages.subject: Re: [BioGeoBEARS] Tree size and phylogenetic sampling
parts:
On Fri, Jul 15, 2016 at 8:15 AM, <lizmil...@gmail.com> wrote:
I have some conceptual questions about BioGeoBears usage. My goal is to use DEC and DEC+J models on a large tree of ~4,000 species, and then break the tree up into small clades and repeat analyses. 

What is the smallest size tree before it becomes unprudent to use this approach, because of loss of power? (As in Davis et al. 2013: BiSSE loses power after ~300 species). I saw in Matzke (2013; PhD thesis) the smallest tree size used in Chapter 3 had 5 species; should I take this to mean models implemented in BioGeoBears are not strongly affected by tree size?

DEC has only 2 free parameters and DEC+J has only 3.  So this is in the zone of models like linear regression, which has parameters for slope, intercept, and error term.  Would you be comfortable with a regression analysis with 5 data points?  Probably that's pushing it.  10 points?  Might be ok.  20 or more?  Probably fine.

Basically, the number of tips in your tree is the number of data points, and (in ML analyses at least) you always want more data than free parameters. 

For small datasets (<50 or so), you should always use AICc instead of AIC to compare models, because AICc has a small-sample-size bias correction.

The 5-species clade analysis (Uma, fringe-toed lizards), has now been published in Van Dam and Matzke (2016), along with a bunch of more speciose clades:

Matthew H. Van Dam, Nicholas J. Matzke
Evaluating the influence of connectivity and distance on biogeographical patterns in the south-western deserts of North America
First published: 3 March 2016
DOI: 10.1111/jbi.12727
http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/jbi.12727/full

If you read the paper, you will see that we comment on how the small size of the Uma phylogeny makes it hard to distinguish between models.  Basically, we report the results we got, but we don't put any weight on them. The paper also compares AIC and AICc results on Uma -- and there are differences, meaning the small sample size is causing problems.

But -- the saving grace of all of this is that small datasets will usually cause small likelihood differences, which means you won't have signficant likelihood ratio tests, and AICc won't show strong relative support for any of the models.  This is the statistics telling you "your data don't have enough power to answer the question".

My group is poorly sampled (maybe 30% of the total number of species). From reading the literature my impression is that there isn't a single common way to deal with incomplete sampling, such as adding sampling fractions to a BiSSE analysis in diversitree. Am I correct in this impression? My immediate thought to deal with this is to randomly prune tips and get some estimate of robustness of the results as if to simulate incomplete sampling (on an already incompletely sampled tree, yes).

You could try that, especially since the tree is so huge.  Basically though what you will see is that as long as ranges are conserved on the tree (sister species tend to have similar ranges -- another way of saying this is that rates of change are substantially less than the rate of observed lineage splitting), there is enough signal to distinguish models. Matzke (2014), SysBio, did an extensive set of SSE simulations to look at the effect of varying amounts of extinction.  Basically extinction didn't change inference or model choice hugely.  This was random extinction though, obviously if you have biogeographically biased extinction (or badly biased sampling), this could have big effects, although that's the case for any comparative phylogenetic method (e.g. if you only sample large species and ignore small ones, this would cause ancestral state estimates to be artificially big!).
Thank you! Sorry for the BiSSE comparisons- I am familiar with BiSSE and diversitree but I am new to biogeographic models.

DEC, DEC+J etc. are all just special cases of ClaSSE -- "E" is set to 0 (extinction is assumed, falsely, to be 0), and speciation is basically state-independent.  So these BioGeoBEARS models are ClaSSE with most of the parameters fixed: 

BioGeoBEARS DEC and DEC+J as special cases of ClaSSE
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-validation#BGB_ClaSSE

Cheers!
Nick
